previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 72-year-old male with a history of systolic heart failure (EF 35%), interstitial lung disease, COPD, lung cancer after Cyberknife therapy, atrial fibrillation, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and orthopnea over three days. Initial evaluation revealed elevated proBNP and engorged pulmonary vessels on chest imaging, consistent with mild volume overload. Despite no significant weight gain or leg swelling, his symptoms were attributed to acute on chronic heart failure, poorly tolerated due to underlying lung disease. He was treated with IV furosemide and transitioned to increased oral torsemide (60 mg daily) and started on lisinopril 2.5 mg daily. Abdominal discomfort was evaluated with CT, which ruled out acute pathology and suggested chronic constipation. His condition improved, he was able to lie flat, and was discharged home after two days. He was advised to continue home medications, use nicotine patch for smoking cessation, monitor weight daily, and follow up with cardiology, pulmonology, and primary care.

# Abdominal Pain: thought seconday to ischemic colitis vs 
mesenteric ischemia.  The patient reports  1.5 months of lower  
abdominal pain, nausea, decreased PO and weight loss. His 
symptoms were felt most likely to mesenteric ischemia or 
ischemic colitis given his risk factor of PVD, active smoking 
and atrial fibrillation  It is  possible that the patient has a 
fixed stenosis of his mesenteric vessels; and experiences pain 
with increased demand to the gut. Also possible that he may be 
showering micro emboli in the setting of afib, although he is 
chronically anticoagulated. He is unable to get a CTA to 
visualize the vessels because of his CKD. A mesenteric dupplex 
was performed, however the study was limited and the mesenteric

obstruction and the patient has been passing gas an moving his

diverticulitis; mass, or bowel wall thickening to suggest 
inflammtion of the colon. Lacate was checked this admission and 
was also normal  His pain was improved at discharge. Medical 
optimization of his risk factors include treating his 
atherosclerotic disease, counseling regarding smoking cessation 
which was done and patient sent home with patches, and 
consideration of echocardiogram to assess for thrombus formation 
as outpatient.

interrogated during this hospitalization and noted an episode of

and orthostatic hypotension  as patient was clinically dry on

unlikely since he had a white count that improved with fluid and

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,
It was a pleasure participating in your care. You were admitted 
to the hospital because you had of your ongoing abdominal pain.  
We think your pain may be from poor blood flow to  the vessels 
in your abdomen which you are at risk for with your history of 
peripheral vascular disease and active smoking. We are unable to 
do  certain imaging ( CT angiogram) that gets  a good look at 
these vessels because of your kidney disease. We did an 
ultrasound of the vessels, but this study wasn't able to get a 
good look at the vessels.  The treatment for this is mostly 
optimizing you medically, which means managing your cholesterol 
with medication, and quitting smoking.

We also noticed that you lost about 5lbs from your dry weight ( 
207 lbs) and  and your kidney numbers were elevated. This is 
likely related to you eating less from the abdominal pain and 
because you are on water pills ( torsemide). We gave you fluid, 
held your diuretics and your kidney numbers improved.  We are 
holding your diuretics at discharge and will  provide you with a 
script to get your kidney numbers checked on ___.  You 
should weigh yourself daily.  If your weight is greater than 
207lbs you should call your cardiologist Dr. ___ to discuss 
what dose of torsemide to restart.

You also reported that you had an episode where you passed out. 
We think this was likely related to your dehydration. We 
interrograted your ICD and there were no abnormal rhythms or 
shocks delievered that correlated with your event. 

Finally, you had a biopsy of the lesion on your liver. Your 
oncologist should be in touch with you regarding the results of 
the biopsy.  Now that the biopsy is done you were restarted on 
coumadin. You should get your INR checked on ___ and Dr. 
___ will let you know if you need to make any changes to 
your dose. 

Your weight at discharge is  203 lbs.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with probable non-small cell carcinoma of lung
with new FDG avid liver lesions on PET-CT ___ // Biopsy of R lateral
superficial liver lesion which is FDG-avid; discussed with Drs. ___,
___ at thoracic conference.

COMPARISON:  Ultrasound ___, PET-CT ___.

PROCEDURE:  Ultrasound-guided targeted liver biopsy.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___, radiology fellow and Dr. ___,
attending radiologist, who was present and supervising throughout the total
procedure time.

FINDINGS: 

Limited preprocedure grayscale and Doppler ultrasound imaging of the liver was
performed. The hypoechoic subcapsular lesion in segment V measuring
approximately 1.5 x 3.5 was identified, targeted for biopsy. A suitable
approach for targeted liver biopsy was determined.

TECHNIQUE:  The risks, benefits, and alternatives of the procedure were
explained to the patient with an interpreter. After a detailed discussion,
informed written consent was obtained. A pre-procedure timeout using three
patient identifiers was performed per ___ protocol.

Based on the pre-procedure imaging, an appropriate skin entry site for the
biopsy was chosen. The site was marked. The skin was then prepped and draped
in the usual sterile fashion. The superficial soft tissues to the liver
capsule were anesthetized with 7 mL 1% lidocaine.

Under real-time ultrasound guidance, a single 18-gauge core biopsy sample was
obtained. The sample was provided to the on-site cytologist who indicated an
adequate sample.

The skin was then cleaned and a dry sterile dressing was applied. There were
no immediate complications.

SEDATION:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
0.25 mg Versed and 12.5 mcg fentanyl throughout the total intra-service time
of 20 minutes during which patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse.

IMPRESSION: 

Uncomplicated 18-gauge targeted liver biopsy x 1, with specimen provided to
the cytologist.
